18221:
Athanasius (about 296-373), bishop of Alexandria and five times exiled for opposing Arianism, wrote *On the Incarnation*. Humanity, made in God's image, was sliding back into corruption and death; only the Word who made us could remake us. By taking a body and offering it in death for all, he defeated death and restored the image (On the Incarnation 6-10). His summary became a watchword of Eastern theology: he became human that we might become divine (54.3). This is the root of theosis (deification): not that people become God by nature, but that by grace they share in God's life and immortality (2 Pet 1:4).

The Cappadocian Fathers, Basil of Caesarea (about 330-379), his brother Gregory of Nyssa (about 335-395) and their friend Gregory of Nazianzus (about 329-390), defended the full divinity of the Son and the Spirit at the council of Constantinople (381). Gregory of Nazianzus argued that what Christ did not assume (take on) he did not heal (*Letter* 101), so Christ must be fully human, mind included. Gregory of Nyssa's *Catechetical Oration* is effectively a handbook on how to explain the faith, including the image of Christ's humanity as bait that caught death and the devil (24), and he too hoped that evil would finally be emptied out. Basil preached against hoarding wealth and founded a large complex for the poor and sick at Caesarea, showing that the gospel was expected to produce mercy.
18222: Chrysostom and Augustine: the preacher and the theologian of grace
18223:
John Chrysostom (about 349-407), 'golden-mouthed', preached through whole books of the Bible in Antioch and then as archbishop of Constantinople, where his blunt preaching against luxury led to his exile and death. His constant themes are repentance, the love of God, care for the poor and serious discipleship for ordinary Christians, not only monks. In his homilies on Matthew he urges hearers not to honour Christ's body with silk in church while neglecting him naked and hungry outside (Homilies on Matthew 50). His Easter sermon, still read in Orthodox churches, proclaims Christ's victory over death; its attribution to him is traditional.

Augustine of Hippo (354-430), a teacher of rhetoric converted in Milan in 386 (Confessions 8.12) and bishop of Hippo in North Africa, shaped Western Christianity more than anyone after Paul. Against Pelagius he taught that humanity is bound by original sin and cannot turn to God without prior grace, which God gives freely (*On the Spirit and the Letter*, 412). In *The City of God* (413-426) he describes two cities formed by two loves, love of God and love of self (14.28), and reads the thousand years of Revelation 20 as the present age of the church (20.7-9), moving the West away from an earthly millennium. He also defended eternal punishment at length (book 21).

With Augustine, the Western gospel focused more sharply on the individual's sin, grace and eternal destiny, while the Eastern tradition kept its accent on incarnation, healing and theosis. Both, however, saw themselves as faithful to the same creed.
18224: What stayed the same, what changed, and how to judge it
18225:
What stayed the same: the story of one Creator God; Jesus as the Messiah and Son, truly human, crucified, raised and coming again; forgiveness of sins; the gift of the Spirit; the call to repent and be baptised; resurrection of the body and final judgment; a life of love, sexual purity and care for the poor. The creeds (Nicaea 325, Constantinople 381) are largely an expansion of the earlier rule of faith.

What new emphases appeared: (1) sacraments, with baptism and Eucharist described in realistic, saving terms; (2) martyrdom, prized as the perfect imitation of Christ; (3) moral rigour and post-baptismal penance; (4) Logos theology, presenting Christ to philosophers; (5) recapitulation and theosis, explaining salvation as the healing and transfiguring of human nature; (6) the institutional church and bishops as guardians of the true gospel; (7) a gradual cooling of imminent end-time hope after Constantine, and Augustine's spiritual reading of the millennium.

How to judge this depends on where you stand. Many Protestants (for example Thomas F. Torrance in *The Doctrine of Grace in the Apostolic Fathers*, 1948) argue that grace was soon overshadowed by moralism. Catholic and Orthodox writers (following John Henry Newman's *Essay on the Development of Christian Doctrine*, 1845) see a faithful unfolding of what was implicit in the apostles. Many historians take a mixed view: real gains in clarity and depth, and some real losses, especially of the kingdom's earthly and communal hope and the simplicity of grace.
18226: Was the gospel 'corrupted' after the apostles? 'Corruption' is itself a judgement. Historians agree that emphases shifted (sacraments, penance, philosophy, hierarchy). They disagree on whether these were decline (many Protestants and restorationists), legitimate development (Catholic and Orthodox), or a mix (many historians across traditions).

18328: The gospel of the kingdom, then and now
18329: How has 'the gospel of the kingdom' been understood from Jesus and the apostles through the Fathers, the Middle Ages, the Reformation and the revivals, to today's movements, and what happened to the hope for 'the restoration of all things'?
18330: Jesus announced that God's kingdom was arriving, and the apostles announced that it had been opened through his death and resurrection and would be completed at his return, when God restores all things (Acts 3:21). Every later age kept parts of this message and stressed some parts more than others. The Fathers stressed the incarnation, sacraments and holy living; the medieval church linked the kingdom with the church and the path of penance to heaven; the Reformers put forgiveness by faith at the centre; revivalists stressed the new birth and personal decision. Modern movements each recover a neglected piece: social justice, new creation, personal conversion, healing and spiritual power, or blessing in this life, and each is criticised for losing another piece. Seeing the whole range helps readers ask which emphases are biblical and which are out of balance, without assuming any one era got everything right or everything wrong.
18331: In the New Testament the kingdom is God's reign, begun in Jesus and completed at his return; personal forgiveness and new creation are both parts of it.
18332: Each era emphasised what its questions demanded and, by critics' accounts, neglected something else.
18333: The phrase 'restoration of all things' (Acts 3:21) has been read as Israel's restoration, cosmic renewal, universal salvation, and a restored church; each reading has serious defenders.
18334: Modern divides (social gospel versus personal salvation, kingdom-now versus future kingdom) often replay older tensions between present and future, individual and cosmic.
18335: Fair comparison means describing each movement as its best representatives would, then noting the strongest criticisms.
18336: Many recent scholars and church statements (for example the Lausanne Covenant, 1974) try to hold proclamation, personal faith and social responsibility together.
18337: The New Testament baseline: already and not yet
18338:
Jesus preached that God's reign had come near and showed it by healing, forgiving and gathering a renewed Israel (Mark 1:14-15; Luke 11:20). The apostles preached that through the cross and resurrection Jesus is now Lord and Messiah, that the Spirit has been poured out, and that he will return to judge and to complete God's purposes (Acts 2:32-36; Acts 10:42). They still preached 'the kingdom' (Acts 8:12; Acts 19:8; Acts 28:23; Acts 28:31) and said believers have already been transferred into the kingdom of God's Son (Col 1:13), yet must enter it through many hardships (Acts 14:22).

The New Testament holds several things together: personal forgiveness and new birth (John 3:3-5; Rom 3:21-26), a new community where social divides are overcome (Gal 3:28; Acts 2:42-47), power over sickness and evil (Acts 3:6-8; Acts 10:38), suffering and the cross (Phil 3:10), and the renewal of the whole creation (Rom 8:19-23; Rev 21:1-5). Most of the story below is about which of these strands each age pulled to the front.
18339: The thread of 'the restoration of all things'
18340:
In Solomon's Portico Peter says heaven must receive Jesus until the time for 'restoring all the things about which God spoke by the mouth of his holy prophets' (Acts 3:21). The Greek word is *apokatastasis*, restoration. Related ideas appear elsewhere: the disciples ask whether Jesus will now restore the kingdom to Israel (Acts 1:6), Elijah is to come and restore all things (Matt 17:11; Mal 4:5-6), Jesus speaks of the 'renewal' (*palingenesia*, rebirth) of all things (Matt 19:28), creation waits to be freed (Rom 8:19-23), God reconciles all things through the cross (Col 1:20), sums up all things in Christ (Eph 1:10), and makes all things new (Rev 21:5).

These texts have been read in at least four ways. (1) The restoration of Israel and fulfilment of the prophets' promises, the reading most commentators prefer because Peter limits the 'all things' to what the prophets spoke. (2) Cosmic renewal: God will heal and renew the whole created order, not discard it (Irenaeus; Abraham Kuyper; N. T. Wright; J. Richard Middleton). (3) Universal restoration of persons: in the end all, or all rational beings, will be reconciled to God (Origen, Gregory of Nyssa, and today David Bentley Hart), a view rejected by most churches and formally condemned in the sixth-century anti-Origenist anathemas. (4) Restoration of the church: Restorationist and some Pentecostal and charismatic groups have used Acts 3:21 for the recovery of New Testament church life, gifts or offices before Christ returns. A fifth, dispensational, reading links it to a future restored Israel in a literal millennium.
18341: Does 'restoration of all things' mean every person will be saved? Universalists cite Acts 3:21 with Col 1:20 and 1 Cor 15:28. Most interpreters answer that Acts 3:23 immediately warns that those who will not listen will be cut off, and that the 'all things' are those promised by the prophets. Both sides agree the text points to a renewed world, not merely souls in heaven.
18342: The Fathers and the medieval church: kingdom, church and the way to heaven
18343:
Early writers such as Justin and Irenaeus expected an earthly reign of Christ and a renewed creation (Justin, *Dialogue* 80-81; Irenaeus, *Against Heresies* 5.32-36). From the third century onward, and decisively with Augustine, the Western church tended to read the kingdom as the church's present life and the millennium as the church age (*City of God* 20.7-9), while the East stressed the incarnation and theosis. After Constantine, as the church became tied to the empire, the line between God's kingdom and Christian society blurred.

In the medieval West the gospel was experienced mainly through the church's sacraments. Baptism washed away original sin; serious later sins were dealt with through confession, absolution and satisfaction; the Fourth Lateran Council (1215) required annual confession and communion; purgatory completed what was lacking before heaven. Anselm's *Why God Became Man* (1098) explained the cross as satisfaction for the honour owed to God. The friars, led by Francis and Dominic, took preaching of penance and imitation of Christ's poverty to the towns. Joachim of Fiore (about 1135-1202) predicted a coming 'age of the Spirit', an early example of hope for a renewed earthly order that later radicals took up.

Defenders point out the period's achievements: hospitals, care of the poor, monastic learning, a whole society shaped by the Christian calendar, and deep devotion to Christ's passion. Critics (above all the Reformers) say the free promise of forgiveness was buried under merit, fear and the church's control of grace.
18344: The Reformation: forgiveness by faith at the centre
18345:
Martin Luther came to see the gospel as God's promise of forgiveness for Christ's sake, received by faith alone, in contrast to the law that demands and condemns. The righteousness of God in Romans 1:17 was, he concluded, the righteousness God gives, not the one he demands. John Calvin called justification 'the main hinge on which religion turns' (*Institutes* 3.11.1), but set it within union with Christ, which also brings sanctification and a calling to serve God in every area of life. The Reformers also believed in Christ's kingdom, which Luther related through his 'two kingdoms' teaching and Calvin through the ordering of church and city.

The Anabaptists (radical reformers) preached the kingdom as a visible community of disciples living by the Sermon on the Mount: believers' baptism, sharing, refusal of the sword. The Catholic Council of Trent (1547) affirmed that justification begins with God's grace and faith but rejected faith alone, teaching that justification includes inner renewal and can grow.

Supporters see the Reformation as the recovery of Paul's gospel of grace. Critics, including some Protestants today, say it framed the gospel so strongly around the individual's guilt and acquittal that the kingdom, the church as community and the renewal of creation receded, a view associated with Krister Stendahl's essay on Paul and 'the introspective conscience of the West' (1963) and the 'New Perspective on Paul'.
18346: Revivalism: new birth, decision and the coming end
18347:
From the 1730s the evangelical revivals put the new birth at the centre (John 3:3-7). John Wesley preached assurance of forgiveness and a life of holiness; George Whitefield preached that outward religion without the new birth cannot save; Jonathan Edwards urged hearers to flee God's wrath. Wesley also preached that animals and the whole creation would share in the final 'general deliverance' (sermon on Romans 8:19-22, 1781), a reminder that revivalists did not all reduce the gospel to individual souls.

In the nineteenth century Charles Finney's 'new measures' (anxious bench, protracted meetings) stressed immediate personal decision, and he linked revival to social reforms such as abolition. Later in the century, under the influence of dispensational premillennialism (J. N. Darby, the Scofield Bible) and the decline of postmillennial optimism, preachers such as D. L. Moody increasingly presented the world as a sinking ship from which individuals must be rescued. Moody is widely reported to have used this lifeboat image, though exact wording varies.

Supporters see an explosion of mission, conversion, Bible reading and reform (for example abolition and prison reform). Critics say the gospel narrowed to a transaction for the individual soul, focused on escaping hell and going to heaven, with the kingdom pushed into the future.
18349:
The social gospel arose in industrial America around 1880-1920. Walter Rauschenbusch, a Baptist pastor in New York's Hell's Kitchen, argued that Jesus' kingdom of God meant transforming society, not only saving souls, and that sin is also built into institutions (*Christianity and the Social Crisis*, 1907; *A Theology for the Social Gospel*, 1917). It inspired labour reforms and later shaped Martin Luther King Jr. Critics, including Reinhold Niebuhr, said it was too optimistic about human progress; conservatives said it lost the cross, sin and conversion. Latin American liberation theology (Gustavo Gutiérrez, *A Theology of Liberation*, 1971) later read the kingdom as God's preference for the poor and liberation from oppression.

In reaction, much twentieth-century evangelicalism focused on personal salvation: God loves you, sin separates you, Christ died for you, receive him by faith. Billy Graham's crusades and Bill Bright's *Four Spiritual Laws* booklet shaped how millions heard the gospel. Supporters stress its clarity, its fidelity to texts like John 3:16 and Romans 10:9, and its fruit in conversions. Critics say it can shrink the kingdom to a private transaction and treat discipleship and justice as optional extras.

The Lausanne Covenant (1974) tried to reconnect the two: evangelism is primary, but Christians also have social responsibility, and both are part of Christian duty (sections 4-6). Many evangelicals now speak of 'integral' or 'holistic' mission, a phrase associated with Latin American evangelicals such as René Padilla and Samuel Escobar.
18350: Myth: the social gospel denied personal faith, and evangelicals ignored social action. Rauschenbusch prayed and preached personal conversion, and nineteenth-century evangelicals led abolition, temperance and relief societies. The sharp split widened in the early twentieth-century modernist-fundamentalist controversy (sometimes called 'the great reversal').
18351: Pentecostal power and the prosperity gospel
18352:
Pentecostalism, sparked by the Azusa Street revival in Los Angeles (1906) under William Seymour, preached a 'full gospel': Jesus as Saviour, Sanctifier, Spirit-baptiser, Healer and soon-coming King. The kingdom was experienced in present power: healing, tongues, prophecy and deliverance (Acts 2:4; Mark 16:17-18; Jas 5:14-15). Later John Wimber's *Power Evangelism* (1986) argued that signs and wonders should accompany preaching as in Jesus' ministry. Pentecostal and charismatic Christianity is now among the largest forms of Christianity worldwide, especially in Africa, Latin America and Asia. Critics (including cessationists) say it can elevate experience over scripture or promise healing God has not promised; supporters reply that it recovered the New Testament's expectation of the Spirit's power.

The prosperity gospel, which grew from healing revivalism and Word of Faith teachers (E. W. Kenyon, Kenneth Hagin, Oral Roberts' 'seed faith', Kenneth Copeland), teaches that Christ's work secured health and material blessing for believers, received by faith and positive confession (3 John 1:2; 2 Cor 8:9; Deut 8:18). Its defenders stress God's goodness, dignity for the poor and faith for practical needs. Critics across traditions, including Pentecostal scholars and the Lausanne Theology Working Group (2008-2009), say it misreads these texts, ignores the cross and suffering (2 Cor 12:7-10; Phil 4:11-13) and can exploit the poor. Historian Kate Bowler (*Blessed*, 2013) gives a fair account of its history and appeal.
